prompt: A prospective client opens the first call with: "We've narrowed it down to two vendors for automating our order-confirmation emails. Which one would you go with?" You know nothing yet about their order process. What's the right first move?

options.text: Ask a few clarifying questions, then give a lean-toward answer so the call feels productive
Say you can't usefully compare either vendor yet, and propose a short scoping pass to see what the confirmation-email step actually has to do first
Recommend whichever vendor has the better reputation, since both are presumably competent
Ask which vendor is cheaper, since cost is the deciding factor between two similar tools

hints: What would change your answer if you knew more about their order process? If the answer is "a lot," you don't have enough to answer yet.
A call that "feels productive" and a call that's actually useful to the client are not always the same call.
explanation: Giving a lean-toward answer to make the call feel productive is the tempting middle option — it avoids the discomfort of saying "I don't know yet" on a first call, which feels like it undersells you. It does the opposite: it trains the client to think you evaluate tools from a spec sheet, which is a service they didn't need to hire a consultant for. Naming that you need a scoping pass before any vendor comparison is worth anything is the harder thing to say and the thing that actually earns the fee — it tells the client what they're paying for.

prompt: Larkspur's owner, after hearing you want two days to map the process before touching any vendor comparison, pushes back: "We already know the problem — verification takes too long. What's there to map?" Write the two or three sentences you'd say back, in a way that doesn't argue with him but also doesn't fold.
hints: He's not wrong that verification takes too long — he's wrong that "too long" tells you where the time goes.
Naming a concrete unknown is more persuasive than asserting that mapping is generally good practice.
You're not asking permission to be thorough. You're explaining what "too long" could mean, and why the answer changes what he should buy.
explanation:
A strong answer agrees with his observation and then names a concrete unknown it doesn't resolve — something like: "You're right that it's too long, and I believe you. What I don't know yet is whether the 20 minutes is mostly keying data, mostly waiting on insurer phone lines, or mostly redoing rejected submissions — and each of those points at a different fix, some of which no software touches. Two days tells me which one you're actually paying for, so the vendor conversation is about the right problem instead of a guess."

The weak version either restates that mapping is best practice (unpersuasive to someone who wants a fast answer) or backs down and starts comparing vendors anyway (which is how you end up owning a tool that didn't fix anything six months later, as the diagnose-mechanism exercise in this lesson showed).

prompt: Match each client statement to the engagement it's actually signalling — read past the word they used for it.

pairs.left: "We just want to know if this is worth pursuing before we spend real money."
pairs.right: Diagnose

pairs.left: "Our dev team is ready to build, they just need to know exactly what to build."
pairs.right: Design

pairs.left: "We don't have anyone in-house who could build this even if we knew what to build."
pairs.right: Deliver

right: No engagement — this is a sales inquiry, not a scoping conversation

hints: Ask what would exist at the end of each engagement, on someone's hard drive, if it went well — a document, a spec, or running software.
"Our dev team needs to know exactly what to build" is telling you who builds it, which tells you what your deliverable has to be instead.
explanation: "Worth pursuing before we spend real money" is a diagnose request — they want the assessment, and the decision to spend more comes after. "Dev team ready to build, needs to know what" is a design request — the deliverable is the spec their team executes, not code from you. "Nobody in-house who could build this" removes the design-only option entirely — if there's no one to hand a spec to, either you build it or nothing gets built, which makes this a deliver engagement once the client decides to proceed. The distractor is there because plenty of first contacts genuinely are just sales inquiries with no scoping content yet — matching one of these three onto a message that's really just "tell us more about what you do" is a common early mistake.

prompt: A client's email says: "We want an automation audit of our customer onboarding process." Their signature block lists them as "Head of Operations," and a follow-up sentence mentions "our two engineers are pretty stretched right now." Write the one clarifying question you'd ask before writing a proposal, and say what answer would point you toward diagnose versus design versus deliver.
hints: "Pretty stretched" could mean the engineers will build it later, or that they have no capacity and need you to build it now — those point at different engagements.
A good clarifying question narrows between two or three concrete outcomes, not between vague levels of "how automated" they want to be.
explanation:
A strong question is concrete and outcome-facing, something like: "When you say audit — are you looking for a written assessment of where automation would help, a build-ready spec your engineers can pick up when they have capacity, or working automation you'd want built for you given they're stretched?" 

An answer naming a written assessment with no build commitment points to diagnose. An answer confirming the two engineers will build once they have a target, even months from now, points to design — your job is producing something precise enough to survive being picked up later by people who weren't in the room. An answer where "stretched" means "we don't have room for this ever" points to deliver, because there's no internal team to hand a spec to.

The weak version of this exercise asks something generic like "what's your budget?" — a real question eventually, but it doesn't distinguish the three engagements, and a client can have the same budget figure in mind for wildly different scopes.

prompt: "If an automated system's accuracy on its own benchmark is high, the overall process it's part of will get faster."

config.statement: A high benchmark accuracy on the automated step guarantees the overall process improves.
config.rubric: Accept answers that identify the gap between step-level accuracy and end-to-end process outcomes — e.g. that a well-performing step can still be gated by an inconsistent upstream input, a downstream matching step, or a queue elsewhere in the process that the automated step never touches.

hints: Think about the Northbeam example: what was the model's own accuracy, and what was the process's overall review rate?
A step being fast and accurate says nothing about what happens right before or right after it in the process.
explanation: False, and the Northbeam case is the concrete version: 96% read accuracy on the document, 40% human review on the overall process, because the constraint was in matching against inconsistent vendor names — a step the model's own benchmark never measured. A benchmark measures the step it was built to measure. It says nothing about whether that step was the process's actual bottleneck, or whether everything upstream and downstream of it still works the way it always did.

prompt: A client wants to automate matching customer support tickets to the right product category, so tickets route to the right team automatically. Before agreeing to scope this, write the three questions from the pre-mortem procedure you'd actually ask them (skip the recommendation step — just the diagnostic questions), specific to this scenario.
hints: Question 1 is about the input: do support tickets arrive with any consistent structure, or is category information buried differently in every ticket?
Question 2 is about the current human workaround: who routes tickets correctly today, and what do they know that isn't written down anywhere?
Question 3 is about scope: is fixing anything upstream of the routing step actually on the table, or is the brief only "automate the routing"?
explanation:
Strong answers name something concrete to this scenario rather than restating the procedure generically. Example: (1) "Do tickets come in through one channel with structured fields, or through email/chat/web-form with category information expressed differently — or absent — in each?" (2) "Who currently decides the category when it's ambiguous, and are they using information that isn't in the ticket text itself — like knowing a customer's account tier or past tickets?" (3) "Is standardizing what information a ticket must contain before routing part of this engagement, or only the routing logic itself?"

A weak answer asks something generic like "what's your current process?" — a fine opening question in general, but it doesn't target the specific failure mode this lesson is about: an automated step inheriting an upstream inconsistency it can't see or fix.

prompt: You recommended an automated system with a written limitation: it should not run unsupervised on cases below a stated confidence threshold. The client's team, six months later, quietly disables the human-review step to save time, doesn't tell you, and a failure occurs. What's the most defensible way to have prevented ending up fully blamed for this, looking back at what you could have done at launch?

options.text: Nothing — once the recommendation is handed over, whatever the client does with it is entirely their responsibility
Build a mechanism that makes the safeguard's status visible or alerts when it's disabled, rather than relying on a limitation clause the client may never re-read under pressure
Refuse to hand over any recommendation that has limitations, since a client might disable a safeguard later
Get the client to sign a longer legal waiver up front covering any future misuse

hints: A written limitation in a document is only as strong as the chance someone re-reads it at the exact moment they're tempted to ignore it.

"Whatever the client does is entirely their responsibility" is true in a narrow legal sense and still leaves you owning the reputational and relationship damage — the goal is preventing the failure, not just being technically blameless after it.
explanation: A signed document establishes what was agreed, but it doesn't prevent the failure — it just clarifies blame after the fact, and blame after the fact is a worse outcome for everyone than the failure not happening. Building the safeguard to fail loudly (an alert when it's disabled, a dashboard flag, anything that surfaces the state of the safeguard to someone besides the person who turned it off) closes the actual gap: a written limitation that only gets read once, at signing, is a much weaker control than a system that makes its own degraded state visible. "Refuse to hand over anything with limitations" is impossible — every real system has limitations, and refusing to name them just removes the paper trail that would otherwise protect you. A longer waiver protects you legally in a dispute and does nothing to prevent the clinic's next patient message from being misrouted.

prompt: You're planning a two-week engagement and want to schedule the synchronous, in-person-energy stages for the slots most likely to be workable, with async stages filling the rest. Put these planning steps in the order that actually protects the schedule.

items: List every stage of the engagement and mark each as synchronous-required or async-possible
Identify which days or times of week have historically been more reliable for you
Schedule the synchronous stages into those higher-reliability slots first, with buffer either side
Fill the remaining time with async stages, which can absorb a bad day without moving a client-facing date
Tell the client which dates are fixed (the synchronous ones) and which are a range (the async ones), instead of presenting every date as equally fixed

hints: You can't protect a slot you haven't identified as needing protection — start by sorting the stages.
The client-facing communication step comes last because it depends on the schedule already being built around your actual constraints, not the other way around.
explanation: Sorting the stages first is what makes every later step possible — without knowing which stages actually require synchronous presence, you can't decide what to protect. Identifying your own reliable windows before scheduling means the protection is based on real patterns, not optimism about "a normal week." Putting synchronous stages into those windows with buffer, then filling the rest with async work, is what makes a bad day absorbable instead of a crisis — an async stage can slide two days without anyone noticing; a missed live interview can't. Telling the client last, once the structure exists, means you're presenting a plan, not asking permission for a limitation — "interviews are the 14th, with report drafting flexible across the following week" sounds like normal project management, because it is.

prompt: You've scoped an engagement with a client and want to build in the async/sync flexibility from this lesson without explaining your health to them. Write the one or two sentences you'd put in the project timeline section of your proposal that accomplish this.
hints: You're not asking for an exception — you're describing normal, competent scheduling practice that happens to also protect you.
Naming a fixed date and a flexible range in the same sentence reads as planning, not as an apology.
explanation: A strong answer sounds like ordinary project management, e.g.: "Stakeholder interviews are scheduled for the week of the 14th, with a two-day flex window built in either side. Data review and the draft report are worked across the following two weeks and will be shared as soon as they're ready within that window." Nothing here discloses anything personal, and nothing here reads as a weaker commitment — it reads as someone who plans realistically, which is a credibility signal, not a liability. The weak version either builds no flexibility in at all (setting up a missed-deadline conversation later) or over-explains with something that invites a question you don't want to answer on a client-facing document.

prompt: "We want to understand where our order-fulfillment process is losing time before we commit to anything." Which engagement?

options.text: Diagnose
Design
Deliver

hints: "Before we commit to anything" is the tell.
What would exist at the end of this — a document, or running software?
explanation: Diagnose. "Before we commit to anything" explicitly puts a decision gate after the assessment, and "understand where we're losing time" is an analysis deliverable, not a build or a spec.

prompt: "Here's our internal engineering roadmap — we need a precise spec for the returns-processing automation so our team can build it next sprint." Which engagement?

options.text: Diagnose
Design
Deliver

hints: Who's doing the building here, based on the sentence?
"So our team can build it" tells you what your deliverable has to be usable by.
explanation: Design. Their own engineering team builds it next sprint — your deliverable is the spec precise enough for them to execute without you, which is exactly what design produces.

prompt: "We have no technical staff and want the invoice-matching automation actually working within two months."

config.statement: This request could be satisfied with a design-only engagement.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that with no technical staff, there's no one to execute a spec — a design-only deliverable would leave the client with a document and nothing running, which doesn't meet 'actually working' or the two-month deadline.

hints: If there's no one in-house to build from a spec, what happens to a design-only deliverable?
explanation: False. With no technical staff, a spec has nobody to execute it — "actually working within two months" requires a deliver engagement, because design-only would hand them a blueprint and a still-broken process.

prompt: Sort each client statement into the engagement it's actually asking for.

items.text: "Tell us honestly whether any of this is worth automating."
"Our contractor needs exact specifications before they'll quote us a build price."
"We tried to build this ourselves twice and failed — just make it work."
"We're not sure if this needs a report or a working system yet — help us figure that out."

hints: "Help us figure that out" is itself a diagnose request — even the uncertainty about which engagement is needed gets resolved by a diagnosis.
explanation: "Tell us honestly whether it's worth automating" and "help us figure out what we need" are both diagnose — the deliverable is clarity, not a spec or software. "Exact specifications before they'll quote a build" is design — someone else builds from your spec. "We tried twice and failed, just make it work" is deliver — they've already ruled out doing it themselves.

prompt: Match each situation to what it signals about engagement scope.

pairs.left: Client's budget line stops after a fixed "assessment fee" with nothing else listed
pairs.right: Diagnose is the actual engagement

pairs.left: Client mentions their in-house team is "ready to go, just waiting on direction"
pairs.right: Design is the actual engagement

pairs.left: Client has zero technical staff and a hard external deadline
pairs.right: Deliver is the actual engagement

right: This is a signal of urgency, not of engagement type

hints: Match on what each detail tells you about who builds what, or whether building happens at all.
explanation: A budget that stops at an assessment fee is a diagnose signal regardless of what the email said. A team "ready to go, just waiting on direction" needs a spec, i.e. design. No technical staff plus a hard deadline rules out design-only, since nobody in-house can execute a spec — that's deliver.

prompt: A client's request is ambiguous about which engagement they want. Put these steps in the order you'd actually take to resolve the ambiguity before writing a proposal.

items: Read the request for explicit or implied signals (budget shape, mention of internal team, prior attempts)
Note which signals are ambiguous or missing
Ask one or two concrete clarifying questions targeting the ambiguous signals specifically
Confirm the engagement type back to the client in writing before scoping

hints: You can't know what to ask about until you've noted what's ambiguous.
Confirming in writing comes last because it depends on the answers to your questions.
explanation: Reading for signals first, then noting the gaps, then asking targeted questions, then confirming in writing — each step depends on the one before it. Skipping straight to a clarifying question without first identifying what's actually ambiguous tends to produce vague questions like "what's your budget," which doesn't resolve engagement type on its own.

prompt: A client's message: "We want you to figure out why our lead-routing is a mess and just fix it — whatever that takes." Identify which engagement(s) this actually spans, and write the one clarifying question that would separate them into phases with a decision point in between.
hints: "Figure out why" and "just fix it" are two different deliverables stapled together, the same pattern as the claims-intake example in lesson two.
A good clarifying question proposes a phase break, not just asks for more detail.
explanation: This spans diagnose ("figure out why it's a mess") and deliver ("just fix it"), with design implied in between. A strong clarifying question proposes the phase break directly: "I'd like to start with a diagnosis — mapping the routing process and finding what's actually broken — and then come back to you with a scoped recommendation before any building starts. Does a fixed-price diagnosis phase first work for you, with the fix scoped separately once we know what it needs to be?" This turns an open-ended "whatever it takes" into two decision points instead of one unbounded one.

prompt: A client asks you to recommend a specific AI vendor for classifying support tickets, on your first call, before you've seen any tickets. What's the judgement-call response?

options.text: Recommend the vendor with the best public reviews, since you can always revise later
Decline to recommend a vendor yet, and propose looking at a sample of real tickets first to see what actually makes classification hard here
Ask the client which vendor they're already leaning toward and confirm that one
Recommend against using AI at all until more research is available

hints: This is the same judgement-versus-tool-pick distinction from lesson one, applied to a new scenario.
A recommendation made before you've seen any real data is a guess wearing an invoice.
explanation: Declining to pick a vendor and proposing to look at real tickets first is the judgement call — it's the only option that gathers evidence before committing. Recommending by public reviews or confirming the client's existing lean both skip straight to a tool pick without diagnosis, the exact mistake from lesson one. Recommending against AI outright is just as ungrounded as recommending for it — both are guesses made without having looked at the actual tickets.

prompt: Larkspur's practice owner insists the documented four-step process is accurate and that Renata's spreadsheet is "just her personal notes, not really part of the process." What's the most useful response?

options.text: Defer to the owner — he runs the practice, so the documented process is the authoritative one
Point out, respectfully, that a spreadsheet load-bearing enough to be titled "DO NOT DELETE" and consulted daily is functionally part of the process, whatever it's officially called
Tell the owner he's wrong about his own business
Ignore the disagreement and map both versions separately without reconciling them

hints: The owner isn't wrong that the handbook exists — he's wrong about what counts as 'the process.'
You're not trying to win an argument, you're trying to get access to accurate information without shutting down the person who has it.
explanation: The useful move names the evidence rather than the disagreement: a spreadsheet that's daily-use and defensively titled is, by definition, part of how the work gets done — regardless of its official status. Framing it that way keeps the conversation about facts rather than about whether the owner is wrong, which tends to go worse. Deferring entirely to the handbook produces a map of a process that doesn't run the business. Telling him he's wrong risks the relationship for no gain. Mapping both without reconciling just defers the actual work to later, at a cost of confusion now.

prompt: During a walkthrough at a different client — a staffing agency — you notice a recruiter has three browser tabs pinned: the official ATS (applicant tracking system), a personal Notion page titled "clients who ghost candidates," and a shared Slack channel called #timesheet-fixes. Write two sentences on what each of these three likely represents, and which one you'd ask to see first.
hints: The ATS is presumably the documented system — what are the other two compensating for?
A channel named after a symptom ("fixes") rather than a process step is a strong tell about where something breaks regularly.
explanation: The ATS is the official, documented system. The personal Notion page is likely tracking a pattern the ATS has no field for — which clients are unreliable about giving feedback, information the recruiter needs but the system doesn't capture, so it lives in a private note instead. The Slack channel named #timesheet-fixes is the strongest signal of the three: a channel named after a recurring problem, rather than after a routine process step, usually means there's a standing workaround for something that breaks often enough to need its own space. That's the one worth asking to see first — a recurring, named failure point is exactly the kind of thing a documented process rarely captures and a map badly needs.

prompt: You want to map how customer refund requests get processed at an online retailer. Which opening question gets you the most useful trace?

options.text: "In general, how do refund requests get handled?"
"Can you pull up the last refund request you personally closed, and walk me through everything that happened to it?"
"What's your average time-to-resolution for refund requests?"
"What does the refund policy document say the process should be?"

hints: Which question invites a memory of a specific event, rather than a summary edited to sound coherent?
A real, recent, specific case is easier to recall accurately than 'in general.'
explanation: "Pull up the last one you personally closed" anchors the answer to a real, specific, recent memory — the exact technique this lesson teaches. "In general, how do refund requests get handled" invites a polished, idealized summary, the same trap as asking Larkspur "how does insurance verification work" instead of tracing Maria D.'s referral. "Average time-to-resolution" is a useful number later but tells you nothing about where time actually goes within that average. "What does the policy document say" gets you the documented process from the previous lesson, not the real one.

prompt: You've traced a single support ticket at a software company: submitted Monday 2pm, sat unassigned until Tuesday 10am, first agent response Tuesday 11am asking a clarifying question, customer replies Wednesday 9am, ticket resolved Wednesday 9:20am. Using the worked-example procedure, name the discrete steps, the single longest gap, who was waiting on whom during it, and whether anything here looks like a near-miss or wasted step.
hints: List the steps as discrete actor actions first — submission, assignment, response, reply, resolution.
The longest gap by far is the unassigned period — who was waiting on whom, and is that wait a process design choice or an accident?
explanation: Discrete steps: (1) ticket submitted, (2) sat unassigned, (3) agent's clarifying question, (4) customer's reply, (5) resolution. The longest gap is Monday 2pm to Tuesday 10am — roughly 20 hours unassigned — during which the customer was waiting on the company with zero visibility into why nothing was happening; this is a queueing gap, not a working gap, since once assigned the ticket resolved in under 20 minutes of actual back-and-forth. The near-miss worth flagging: the entire delay was queue time, not work time — the actual resolution, once someone looked at it, took 20 minutes total across both messages. That's a strong signal the bottleneck is assignment/triage, not agent skill or process complexity, which is exactly the kind of finding a single traced ticket surfaces that an 'average resolution time' metric would hide inside one number.

prompt: "If staff report a task takes 20 minutes, the process that task is part of takes roughly 20 minutes end to end."

config.statement: Reported touch time is a reliable estimate of total end-to-end process time.
config.rubric: Accept answers distinguishing touch time (active work) from wait/queue time (sitting between handoffs), and noting that staff estimates almost always report only touch time, which can be a small fraction of the true elapsed time.

hints: What did Maria D.'s 20-minutes-of-touch-time referral actually take end to end?
explanation: False. Staff estimates of 'how long something takes' almost always describe touch time — the part that feels like work — while the process's true elapsed time includes queues and handoff delays that don't feel like anything to report, because nobody's actively doing something during them. Maria D.'s referral was 20 minutes of touch time inside a six-business-day process.

prompt: At a mid-size accounting firm, you're told expense report approvals "usually take a day or two." You trace one report: submitted by an employee Monday 9am, sits in the approving manager's queue until the manager happens to open their approvals inbox Wednesday 4pm, approved in under a minute once seen. Diagnose the actual mechanism causing the delay, and name what kind of fix would target it (without picking a specific tool).
hints: Where's the touch time here, and where's the wait time? They're wildly mismatched.
The manager did nothing wrong by taking a minute to approve it — the question is why it sat unseen for two days first.
explanation: The touch time is under a minute; the entire one-to-two-day delay is queue time spent waiting for the manager to happen to open an inbox they don't check on any fixed schedule. This is the same pattern as the referral handoff: the delay isn't about anyone's competence or the approval decision itself, which is nearly instant once made — it's an invisible queue with no trigger to surface it promptly. A fix that targets the actual mechanism would be something that notifies the manager or otherwise makes a pending approval visible without relying on them remembering to check, rather than anything aimed at making the approval decision itself faster, since the decision was never the slow part.

prompt: Mid-way through a live map-drawing session, a front-desk staff member says "actually, that's not quite right" about a box you just drew. What's the right response?

options.text: Thank them, ask them to explain what actually happens, and redraw the box on the spot
Note it down to review later, so the session stays on schedule
Ask if they're sure, since the information came from someone else in an earlier interview
Move on and address it at the end if there's time

hints: This is the exact moment the whole session was designed to produce — what happens if you don't act on it immediately?
Deferring a correction signals, even unintentionally, that it wasn't actually welcome.
explanation: Fixing it on the spot is the entire point of building the map live and visibly draft — this is the correction the session was designed to surface, and acting on it immediately reinforces that contradiction is genuinely welcome, which makes the next person more likely to speak up too. Noting it for later, questioning their certainty, or deferring to the end of the session all send the opposite signal: that the invitation to correct was polite phrasing rather than a real openness to being wrong, which tends to shut down further corrections for the rest of the session.

prompt: You've drawn a first-draft map of a warehouse's inbound-shipment receiving process as a single straight line: truck arrives, dock worker scans items, items shelved, inventory updated. Before showing it to the receiving team, name two questions you'd ask yourself about what this map might be hiding, based on this lesson's pattern.
hints: The flaw in the Larkspur map was a missing branch at the one place the real process diverges — where might this map be hiding a similar branch?
Think about what happens when something doesn't scan correctly, or doesn't match the expected order.
explanation: Strong questions target the same shape of flaw as the Larkspur example: (1) "What happens when an item doesn't scan correctly, or the shipment doesn't match what was ordered — is there a rejection or exception path this single line is hiding?" (2) "Does 'items shelved' happen the same way every time, or are there cases — damaged goods, wrong quantity, missing paperwork — that branch off into a different, probably slower path this map doesn't show?" A weak answer asks something generic like "is this map detailed enough?" without targeting the specific failure mode from the lesson: a single-path map hiding the branch where the real process most often diverges.

prompt: Sort each reported issue into whether it belongs on the process map as a real, named branch, or is noise not worth mapping.

items.text: A vendor invoice format changes for one specific supplier every month due to a known billing-system quirk on their end
A single data-entry typo caused one order to ship to the wrong address, discovered and fixed the same day
Roughly 15% of customer support tickets are routinely misrouted to the wrong team due to a known keyword-matching flaw
An employee was out sick for a week and their tasks were covered ad hoc by a colleague

hints: Ask: will this specific thing happen again, in roughly the same way, on a predictable basis?
A one-time human absence or single typo is an event. A known system quirk recurring monthly is a pattern.
explanation: The invoice format quirk and the 15% ticket misrouting are both recurring, predictable, and tied to a known, stable cause — exactly what belongs as a real branch. The single typo and the one-week sick coverage are one-off events with no reason to expect the same specific thing to recur in the same form — noise for mapping purposes, however disruptive they felt at the time.

prompt: You're mapping a returns process for an online furniture retailer. A team member describes an exception: about 12% of returns are damaged-in-transit claims, and the specific evidence required (photos, packaging condition, carrier report) varies depending on which carrier delivered it and how the customer describes the damage. Using the case-sim's 'map the pattern, not every instance' approach, write the one or two sentences you'd actually put in the map for this branch.
hints: Name the branch, its rough frequency, and the fact that the specific requirement varies — without listing every combination of carrier and damage type you've ever seen.
The goal is capturing that this branch is common and inherently variable, in a way someone reading the map later can act on.
explanation: A well-pitched map entry names the frequency, the trigger, and the honest fact of unpredictability without enumerating every variation: "Damaged-in-transit claims (~12% of returns): evidence required varies by carrier and reported damage type, and isn't fully predictable in advance — treat as a branch requiring case-by-case evidence review rather than a fixed checklist." This captures what matters for later decisions — that this is common enough to plan around, and variable enough that a rigid rule-based checklist would likely fail — without listing every carrier-damage combination the team member could recall, which would bloat the map without adding decision-relevant information.

prompt: A manager says "our onboarding process is documented in the handbook and everyone follows it." You then notice three different team leads each keep their own private onboarding checklist. What should you conclude?

options.text: The manager is right, and the private checklists are irrelevant duplicates
The existence of three separate private checklists is itself evidence the handbook doesn't fully cover what team leads need — worth investigating before trusting the handbook as the real process
The private checklists should be deleted to enforce one standard process

hints: Three independently-created private checklists is a strong signal, not noise.
explanation: Three team leads independently building their own checklists is a strong shadow-process signal — each of them found the handbook insufficient for their actual needs, and independently arrived at similar workarounds. That's worth mapping before assuming the handbook describes the real process.

prompt: Write the single question you'd ask to start tracing one specific instance of a process, rather than asking for a general description — apply it to "how do you handle a customer complaint."
hints: Anchor to a specific, recent, real memory.
explanation: A strong version: "Can you pull up the last customer complaint you personally handled, and walk me through exactly what happened, in order, with roughly how long each part took?" This anchors to a real memory instead of inviting a polished summary of the ideal case.

prompt: "A process step that takes a long time in total must involve a lot of active human work."

config.statement: Long total elapsed time implies a lot of touch time.
config.rubric: Accept answers distinguishing touch time from wait/queue time, noting that most elapsed time in administrative processes is typically waiting, not active work.

hints: Think about Maria D.'s referral: six business days elapsed, roughly 20 minutes of actual work.
explanation: False. Most elapsed time in administrative processes is queue and wait time, not active work — a step can take days in total while involving only minutes of actual human effort, as Maria D.'s referral trace showed directly.

prompt: Match each mapping mistake to what it actually causes.

pairs.left: Presenting a fully polished, finished-looking map in the review meeting
pairs.right: Team nods instead of correcting errors

pairs.left: Mapping only the happy path with no exception branch
pairs.right: Map looks accurate but hides where most real effort goes

pairs.left: Enumerating every one-off variation of a rare exception in exhaustive detail
pairs.right: Map becomes cluttered and hard to act on

right: Map takes longer to draw but is otherwise unaffected

hints: Each mistake has a distinct, specific consequence covered in this module's lessons.
explanation: A polished map invites nodding, not correction — the fix is a visibly draft artefact. A happy-path-only map hides where effort actually concentrates, since exceptions often consume more real time than the common case. Enumerating every rare variation clutters the map with noise instead of capturing the recurring pattern.

prompt: Put these process-mapping steps in the order this module actually teaches them.

items: Identify shadow-process signals (personal spreadsheets, sticky notes, hedge phrases)
Trace two or three specific real instances end to end, recording elapsed time between steps
Separate touch time from wait time and locate where the queues actually are
Draw a draft map in the team's own words and invite live correction
Add branches only for recurring, predictable exceptions — not one-off events

hints: You can't trace a real instance until you know where the shadow process lives.
Branches for exceptions come last, once the core map exists and has been corrected.
explanation: Spotting shadow-process signals tells you where the real information lives before you trace anything. Tracing real instances gives you the raw timeline data. Separating touch time from wait time is how you read that data for where the actual delay sits. Drawing the draft map and inviting correction turns the traced data into a shared, validated artefact. Only then does adding exception branches make sense, once the core happy-path map is confirmed accurate.

prompt: While mapping a payroll process, an employee mentions "the time our HR software had a five-minute outage during a migration eighteen months ago and we had to process everything by hand." Should this become a branch on the map?

options.text: Yes — any disruption to the process is worth capturing
No — a single historical outage during a one-time migration isn't a recurring, predictable pattern

hints: Will this specific thing happen again, in this form, on a predictable basis?
explanation: No. A one-time software migration outage eighteen months ago is a historical event, not a recurring feature of the process — it fails the same test the power-outage example failed in this module: memorable, but not predictive of anything that will recur.

prompt: A hotel's housekeeping team says room-turnover "usually takes about 30 minutes." You trace one room: cleaner finishes at 11:15am, room sits marked as not-yet-inspected until 1:40pm when a supervisor happens to walk by, inspection takes 4 minutes, room goes live in the booking system at 1:50pm. Diagnose where the actual time went and what kind of fix would target the real bottleneck.
hints: Compare the reported '30 minutes' (touch time) to the actual gap from cleaning-finished to room-live.
The inspection itself was fast — where was the delay?
explanation: The reported 30 minutes describes the cleaner's actual touch time, which is roughly accurate for the cleaning itself. The real elapsed time from clean-finished to room-live was over two and a half hours, almost entirely spent waiting for a supervisor to happen to walk by and notice the room needed inspection — the inspection itself took four minutes once it started. A fix aimed at making cleaning faster would target the wrong step entirely; the actual bottleneck is an unmanaged queue between 'cleaning finished' and 'someone notices it needs inspecting,' the same invisible-handoff pattern as the Larkspur referral-to-spreadsheet gap. A fix should target visibility into that queue, not the cleaning process itself.

prompt: A staff member says, "Honestly, most of us just kind of remember which suppliers cause problems — I don't know if that's useful to you." What's the best response?

options.text: "Okay, thanks — let's move on to the next part of the process."
"That's extremely useful, actually — tell me more about which suppliers, and how you learned to remember them."
"You should probably write that down somewhere official."
"Is that documented anywhere?"

hints: "I don't know if that's useful" is a hedge, not a real assessment of usefulness — the interviewer's response determines what happens next.
The strongest response affirms the value and asks for more, immediately.
explanation: Affirming the value directly and asking for more keeps the door open at exactly the moment it's ajar. Moving on treats the hedge as a dead end, confirming their doubt that it wasn't relevant. Telling them to document it changes the subject to process improvement instead of learning what they actually know right now. "Is that documented anywhere" is a closed question whose likely answer — no — can read as a mild judgment, and it doesn't invite them to actually share the tacit knowledge itself.

prompt: You're about to interview a warehouse team about their picking process, and you know from the client's ops manager that there's been recent anxiety about "automation taking jobs" circulating among staff. Write the two or three sentences you'd open the interview with to address this directly, before asking a single process question.
hints: Naming the anxiety directly, rather than hoping it doesn't come up, tends to work better than ignoring it.
Be honest about what you can and can't promise — false reassurance is its own kind of trust-breaker if it turns out untrue.
explanation: A strong opening names the concern honestly without overpromising, something like: "I know there's been some worry that this project is about replacing people — I want to be upfront that my job right now is just understanding how the work actually happens, including all the workarounds and judgment calls that make it run. What gets recommended later, and what happens with any of it, isn't something I'm deciding today, and I'll be straightforward with you about that as it develops." This addresses the fear-of-automation reason from the lesson directly, without making a promise about outcomes you can't actually guarantee — false reassurance that later turns out untrue costs more trust than an honest, bounded statement upfront.

prompt: Which of these is a genuine story question, not a summary question in disguise?

options.text: "Is the current handoff process between shifts working smoothly?"
"Would you say handoffs are usually clean or usually messy?"
"Tell me about the last shift handoff you were part of, from when it started to when you felt confident you had everything you needed."
"On a scale of one to five, how would you rate shift handoffs?"

hints: Which option anchors to one specific, bounded, retrievable event rather than an overall rating?
explanation: The third option asks for one specific, bounded episode — the last handoff, with a clear start and end point defined by the question itself. The other three all ask for an overall evaluation compressed into a word, a category (clean/messy), or a number — all of which strip out the retrievable detail a real memory would carry.

prompt: Rewrite this question using the worked-example procedure: "Does the current inventory system give you accurate counts?" Show all four steps briefly: the abstraction, the concrete event underneath it, the story rewrite, and what detail it should surface.
hints: The abstraction is 'accurate' — what specific event happens when the count turns out to be wrong?
The story version should anchor to the last time a count was actually checked against reality.
explanation: A strong answer: (1) Abstraction — 'accurate' is an overall judgment about the system's reliability. (2) Concrete event underneath it — someone checks the system's count against a physical count, and it either matches or doesn't. (3) Story rewrite — "Tell me about the last time you physically counted something and it didn't match what the system said. What did you do?" (4) Likely surfaced detail — how often this actually happens, what the discrepancy tends to look like (short, long, specific categories of item), and whether there's an existing workaround for reconciling it, none of which "does it give you accurate counts" would have prompted, since it's easy to answer that with a quick 'yeah, pretty much' without ever recalling a specific mismatch.

prompt: After the case-sim's honest-bounded answer, Renata volunteers a new, useful detail unprompted. What does this pattern most likely indicate?

options.text: She simply forgot to mention it earlier
An honest, non-reassuring answer to her direct question built enough trust that she felt safer volunteering additional real information
The detail isn't actually relevant and she's just filling silence

hints: Compare this to the fear-of-automation reasons for withholding information from lesson one of this module.
What changed between the first two interviews, where this detail wasn't mentioned, and this one?
explanation: This is the direct payoff of handling the direct question honestly — trust that you'll tell her the truth, including uncomfortable truths, makes it safer to volunteer more of what she actually knows, which is exactly the shadow-process and tacit-knowledge information this whole module is built to surface. 'She forgot' doesn't explain why it surfaces specifically after this exchange rather than randomly; treating it as irrelevant filler misses that unprompted volunteered detail, especially about a judgment call she makes routinely, is usually a sign of increased comfort, not decreased relevance.

prompt: You've sent an async prompt: "Please describe how you handle scheduling conflicts." A staff member replies: "We just figure it out as it comes up." What went wrong with the original prompt, using this lesson's terms?

options.text: It should have been sent as a phone call instead
It's a generic, summary-shaped prompt rather than a story-shaped one anchored to a specific instance — the fix is the same rewrite from earlier in this module, applied in writing
The staff member didn't take it seriously

hints: Compare this prompt's shape to "describe your experience with the process" from the build-it exercise.
The fix doesn't require switching format — it requires the same story-versus-summary rewrite as a live interview question.
explanation: The prompt asks for a general description of how conflicts are handled, which invites exactly the compressed non-answer it got — the same failure as any summary question, live or written. A story-shaped rewrite, like "tell us about the last scheduling conflict you had to resolve — what happened and how did you handle it," would anchor to a specific retrievable instance instead. Nothing here indicates the format itself (async vs. live) was the problem, or that the staff member wasn't engaging in good faith — the question just asked for a summary, and got one.

prompt: You've collected async screen recordings from four staff members about how they process returns, and one recording shows a staff member pausing for several seconds before a specific step, with no explanation in the narration. In a live interview you'd ask about that pause immediately. What do you do about it in an async workflow, and what should you honestly note if you can't fully resolve it?
hints: This is exactly the real-time-probe limitation named in this lesson — what's the best available substitute?
If the light follow-up doesn't fully resolve it, what's the honest thing to write in your notes rather than guessing?
explanation: The right move is the light follow-up loop from the build-it exercise: send a short, specific message pointing at the exact moment ("around 0:42 in your recording, you paused before submitting — was something making you double-check there, or just an interruption?") rather than a vague general question. If the reply doesn't fully resolve it — maybe they don't remember, or the explanation is thin — the honest note in your findings is something like "a hesitation was observed at this step; async follow-up didn't fully clarify the cause, and this may be worth a live spot-check if the step turns out to matter for the automation decision," rather than inventing a confident explanation for something you don't actually know. This is the same honesty this module's third lesson modeled with Renata — naming a real limitation plainly instead of papering over it with a guess.

prompt: Sort each note fragment from an interview into quote, observation, or inference.

items.text: "Honestly, some days I just call and hope for the best."
She paused for about five seconds before answering the question about denial rates
She seems uncomfortable discussing how often claims get denied
"We had three denials last week, I think, maybe four."
Two staff members exchanged a glance when the topic of the new software came up
The team is skeptical about whether the new software will actually help

hints: A quote is exact words in quotation marks. An observation is something seen or heard that isn't speech. An inference is your conclusion about what either of those means.
"Seems uncomfortable" and "is skeptical" are both your read on the situation, not things anyone said or a plain fact you witnessed.
explanation: The two quoted sentences are exact words, marked as such. The pause and the exchanged glance are directly witnessed, non-speech events — genuine observations. "Seems uncomfortable" and "is skeptical" are both interpretive conclusions drawn from the quotes and observations around them — real inferences, and possibly correct ones, but categorically different from what was actually said or seen, and they need to be labeled as your reading of the situation rather than presented as flat fact.

prompt: During an interview, a staff member says: "I mean, I guess it works, most of the time," while looking down at their desk and tapping a pen. Write three separate note entries — one quote, one observation, one inference — for this single moment, each clearly labeled.
hints: The quote is only the exact words. The observation is the physical behavior. The inference is what you think it means, labeled as your interpretation.
explanation: A strong answer keeps the three genuinely separate: Quote — "'I mean, I guess it works, most of the time.'" Observation — "Looked down at desk, tapped pen repeatedly while answering." Inference (labeled as such) — "Possible discomfort or lack of confidence in the answer given — worth following up on directly rather than treating 'it works most of the time' as a settled, confident assessment." The key discipline is that the inference is explicitly marked as a possible reading, not stated as established fact, and it's kept in its own line rather than blended into the quote or observation.

prompt: "A reasonable, likely-correct inference about how someone feels is safe to write into a client-facing report as a stated fact, since it's probably true."

config.statement: A likely-correct inference can be presented in a report as if it were a directly established fact.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that inferences, however reasonable, need to be presented as interpretation rather than fact — because they're not defensible as evidence if challenged, and conflating the two undermines the credibility of genuinely evidenced findings in the same report.

hints: What happens if a client's operations director asks 'who actually said that' about a claim that was really your inference?
explanation: False. Even a reasonable, probably-correct inference is a conclusion, not evidence — presenting it as flat fact means it can't survive the question "who said that" or "how do you know," and a report caught overstating one inference as fact tends to lose credibility for its genuinely evidenced findings too. The fix isn't to drop inferences from the report — they're often the most useful part — it's to label them plainly as interpretation, e.g. "based on X and Y, it appears that..." rather than stating them as settled fact.

prompt: "Don't you think automation would make your job easier?" What's wrong with this question as an interview prompt?

options.text: It's a leading question — it signals the expected answer and makes disagreement socially awkward
It's too short
It should be asked earlier in the interview

hints: 'Don't you think' presupposes the answer before the person has said anything.
explanation: "Don't you think" bakes the expected answer into the question itself, making a genuine 'no, actually' feel like disagreeing with the interviewer rather than just answering honestly — the same trust-and-safety issue as this module's first lesson, applied to question phrasing rather than framing.

prompt: Rewrite this leading question into a neutral, story-shaped one: "You'd agree the current process is pretty inefficient, right?"
hints: Remove the presupposition entirely and anchor to a specific instance instead.
explanation: A strong rewrite removes both the leading framing and the summary shape: "Walk me through the last time this process took longer than you expected — what happened?" This neither presupposes inefficiency nor asks for an overall judgment; it asks for a specific retrievable case and lets the person's own account reveal whatever's actually there.

prompt: "Someone hedging with 'that's probably not relevant' before mentioning something is usually a sign the information really isn't relevant."

config.statement: A hedge like 'probably not relevant' reliably predicts the information is actually unimportant.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting the hedge is more often a social test of whether disclosure is welcome, not an accurate self-assessment of relevance — per the Renata spreadsheet example.

hints: Recall Renata's own hedge about her spreadsheet in this module's first lesson.
explanation: False. A hedge like this is much more often a tentative test of whether disclosure is welcome than an accurate judgment of relevance — Renata's own spreadsheet, hedged with almost the identical phrase, turned out to be one of the most useful pieces of information in the whole engagement.

prompt: Sort each interview note fragment into quote, observation, or inference.

items.text: "It's fine, I've just done it so many times I don't think about it."
Sighed audibly before answering the third question about workload
Appears burned out on this specific task, possibly more than they're saying directly
Checked their phone twice during a five-minute answer

hints: Exact words in quotes = quote. Physical behavior witnessed = observation. Your read on what it means = inference.
explanation: The exact words are a quote. The sigh and the phone-checking are both directly witnessed, non-speech behaviors — observations. "Appears burned out, possibly more than they're saying" is your interpretive conclusion — an inference, and one that should be labeled as such rather than presented as an established fact.

prompt: Match each async interview design choice to its actual effect.

pairs.left: Sending a generic written form with the same summary questions as a live script
pairs.right: Produces the same compressed, low-detail answers as any summary question

pairs.left: Requesting a short screen recording of the task with narration
pairs.right: Captures procedural detail a written summary would strip out

pairs.left: Building in a single light follow-up reply instead of zero or unlimited follow-up
pairs.right: Recovers most of the value of live follow-up without an unreasonable burden

right: Guarantees the same rapport as a live conversation

hints: Each choice's effect was covered explicitly in the build-it exercise from this module's fourth lesson.
explanation: A generic written form inherits the summary-question problem regardless of format. A screen recording captures actual procedural detail, not just a description of it. A single light follow-up recovers most of the value of live follow-up questions without demanding an unreasonable amount of unpaid effort. None of these, however well designed, guarantee the same rapport a live conversation builds — that's a real limitation named explicitly in the lesson, not something any of these choices fully solves.

prompt: Put these interview-notetaking steps in the order that keeps quotes, observations, and inferences properly separated.

items: Write down the exact words spoken, in quotation marks, as close to verbatim as possible
Separately note any directly witnessed non-speech behavior (pauses, glances, tone)
Only after both of those, write your own interpretation, explicitly labeled as an inference
When writing up findings later, keep the same three-way labeling rather than blending them into flat statements

hints: Inference has to come after quote and observation, since it's a conclusion drawn from them.
The labeling discipline needs to survive into the final written findings, not just the raw notes.
explanation: Quotes and observations are the raw evidence, captured first and separately since they're two different kinds of witnessed information. Inference comes after, explicitly labeled as your own conclusion drawn from that evidence. Carrying the same three-way separation into final findings, rather than letting it collapse into flat statements during write-up, is what keeps the eventual report defensible against "who actually said that."

prompt: A colleague interviewing alongside you writes in their shared notes doc: "The team clearly doesn't trust the new scheduling software." Write the one question you'd ask them to help separate quote/observation from inference here.
hints: What would you need to know to tell whether 'clearly doesn't trust' is a quote, an observation, or their own conclusion?
explanation: A strong question directly targets the ambiguity: "What did someone actually say or do that led you to write 'clearly doesn't trust' — was that someone's words, or your read on the room?" This doesn't accuse the colleague of doing anything wrong; it simply asks them to trace their own conclusion back to its evidence, which is exactly the discipline this module teaches for your own notes.

prompt: A staff member being interviewed about a task that might be automated asks you point-blank: "Be honest — is this going to cost people their jobs?" You genuinely don't know yet. What's the best response, per this module?

options.text: "Absolutely not, don't worry."
"I can't discuss that, let's continue."
"I honestly don't know yet — I'll tell you straight once I do, instead of guessing now."

hints: This is the same case-sim scenario as Renata's direct question in this module's third lesson.
explanation: An honest, bounded answer — genuine uncertainty plus a commitment to tell the truth once it's known — is what this module's third lesson showed builds trust and eventually more disclosure, without making a promise that might not hold. A false reassurance risks being caught out later; refusing to engage reads as confirmation of the worst fear.

prompt: A client tells you their new ticket-routing automation "cut our response time in half." What's the first thing to check before treating this as a usable figure?

options.text: Whether the automation vendor's marketing materials support a 50% claim
Whether there's an actual recorded measurement of response time before the automation went live to compare against
Whether the client's competitors have seen similar improvements
Whether the client is satisfied with the new response times

hints: "Cut in half" is a comparison claim — what does it need to be a comparison against?
Satisfaction and vendor marketing are both real signals of something, but neither one is a measurement of the before-state.
explanation: "Cut in half" only means something if there's an actual before-measurement to halve — checking for that pre-automation baseline is the first and most important question, because without it, the claim is unverifiable regardless of how satisfied the client feels or what the vendor's materials say. Satisfaction is real but is a different, softer kind of evidence than a measured time comparison. Competitor comparisons and vendor marketing don't establish anything about this specific client's actual before-and-after numbers.

prompt: A prospective client, before you've started any work, says: "We're confident this project will save us about 15 hours a week — can you just confirm that estimate for us?" Write the two or three sentences you'd say back that address the actual problem with the request, without simply refusing.
hints: The problem isn't that 15 hours is unbelievable — it's that 'confirming' a number implies checking it against something, and there's nothing to check it against yet.
Propose the actual next step rather than just declining the request.
explanation: A strong answer names the gap and proposes the fix: "I can't confirm that number yet, because 'saves 15 hours' is a comparison, and right now we only have one side of it — what you expect afterward. What I'd want to do first is measure what the process actually costs today, so that whatever number comes out the other side is something we can both actually check, rather than something either of us is hoping is true." This doesn't dismiss their estimate — it may well turn out close — it just refuses to treat an unmeasured guess as something that can be 'confirmed' without a baseline to confirm it against.

prompt: Match each baseline metric to what it actually measures.

pairs.left: Volume
pairs.right: How many requests move through the process in a given period

pairs.left: Time
pairs.right: Active work (touch time) and total elapsed time including queues

pairs.left: Error rate
pairs.right: How often the process fails on first attempt and needs to be redone

pairs.left: Rework
pairs.right: The average number of touches a request needs before it resolves

right: How satisfied staff feel about the process overall

hints: Each definition should match one of the four metrics precisely, without overlap.
explanation: Volume is a count over a period. Time splits into touch time and total elapsed time, distinguishing active work from queueing. Error rate is specifically about first-attempt failure requiring redo. Rework is the average touches-per-request across the whole distribution, including both the majority that succeed on the first try and the minority that need several. Staff satisfaction is a real and useful thing to know but isn't one of these four precisely-defined baseline numbers.

prompt: A restaurant's online-order system logs 60 orders from one week: 52 went straight to the kitchen without issue, 6 needed a manual correction (wrong address or missing item flagged by staff), 2 were cancelled and fully redone. Using the worked-example procedure, compute total 'touches' if a clean order counts as 1, a corrected order counts as 2, and a redone order counts as 3 — then state the average rework rate and one thing it doesn't tell you.
hints: Sum: 52×1 + 6×2 + 2×3, then divide by 60.
What would you need to know beyond this single average to act on it — which orders, which cause?
explanation: Total touches: 52×1 + 6×2 + 2×3 = 52 + 12 + 6 = 70. Average rework rate: 70 ÷ 60 ≈ 1.17 touches per order. This number, on its own, doesn't say what's causing the corrections and cancellations — whether it's a specific input field prone to errors, a particular time of day, or a specific delivery partner's data feed — which would need a further breakdown of the 8 problem orders specifically, not something the single average can tell you by itself.

prompt: "Using another comparable location's measured rate as a substitute for a location with no data is a defensible estimation technique."

config.statement: Borrowing a comparable site's measured number is an acceptable substitute when the target site has no data of its own.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that different locations can have meaningfully different underlying conditions (insurer mix, staff experience, patient volume), so a borrowed number isn't actually measuring the thing in question — it's substituting a different, real number for an honest estimate of the right one.

hints: Would Renata's location and the new location necessarily see the same insurers in the same proportions?
explanation: False. Even two locations in the same practice can have meaningfully different conditions — insurer mix, staff tenure, patient volume — that change the actual rate. Presenting a borrowed number as this location's baseline substitutes a real, measured-but-wrong-context number for an honest estimate of the right context, which is worse than a clearly-labeled estimate because it looks more authoritative than it deserves to.

prompt: A small nonprofit wants a baseline for how often donor thank-you letters go out late (defined as more than 5 business days after a donation), but they've never tracked this and have no consistent digital record — donations come in through three different channels (mail, a web form, an in-person event system) with no unified log. Propose a specific, defensible estimation approach, naming which of this lesson's three techniques you'd use and why, given this specific constraint.
hints: With three disconnected channels and no existing digital trail, is retrospective sampling realistic, or does the fragmentation push you toward a different technique?
Consider whether a short forward-looking tally might actually be more reliable here than trying to reconstruct three different historical records.
explanation: A strong answer reasons about the specific constraint rather than defaulting to one technique: with three disconnected channels and no unified historical log, retrospective sampling would require separately reconstructing three different partial records, which is slow and likely incomplete — probably a weaker choice here than a two-to-three-week forward-looking manual tally, where someone logs, by hand, the donation date and thank-you-sent date across all three channels going forward. This produces a real, representative, and relatively low-effort measurement rather than trying to painstakingly and unreliably reconstruct fragmented history. A structured recall estimate with a stated range could serve as a rough placeholder while the tally runs, explicitly labeled as a low-confidence interim figure.

prompt: A warehouse manager says a picking error that gets caught and corrected before shipping "costs nothing, since the customer never even sees it." What's the strongest response, applying this lesson's distinction?

options.text: Agree — if the customer never sees it, there's genuinely no cost

Point out that the cost is absorbed by whoever catches and corrects it — their time, and any delay it adds to that shipment leaving on schedule — even though it never reaches the customer or shows up as a customer complaint
Argue the customer probably does notice, even if they don't complain

hints: 'The customer never sees it' answers a different question than 'did this cost anything' — who actually spent time and effort catching and fixing it?
explanation: The correction itself has a real cost — someone's time catching it, someone's time fixing it, and any delay it introduces to that order's schedule — none of which requires the customer to ever notice. This is the same invisible-but-real cost pattern as Larkspur's rejections: absorbed by staff time and process delay rather than showing up as a customer-facing problem, which is exactly why it's easy to dismiss as costless. Speculating about whether the customer secretly notices sidesteps the actual, provable cost that already exists regardless of customer awareness.

prompt: You're presenting a finding to a client: an average of 3 minutes per customer service call is spent on hold while the agent looks up account information in a separate, unlinked system. The client's response is "three minutes isn't much." Using the case-sim's approach, write how you'd present the cost of this in a way that's concrete and honestly scoped, not inflated.
hints: Pick one specific, traceable consequence of the three minutes, not just a stretched extrapolation.

Pair a real number (calls per day × 3 minutes, honestly stated) with a concrete example of what that adds up to for a specific person's day, without overreaching into a dramatic annual dollar figure you can't fully support.
explanation: A strong presentation pairs a modest, honestly-scoped extrapolation with a concrete human consequence, without overreaching: "Across roughly 80 calls a day, that's about four hours of agent time each day spent on hold looking up account information — for one agent handling a full shift of calls, that's most of an extra half a workday spent waiting rather than talking to customers. It also means the customer is sitting in silence for three minutes at the start of every call, which is often exactly the point they decide to hang up and call back later, adding a second full call to the total." This stays within what the data actually supports (calls-per-day × minutes, a real and checkable multiplication) and adds one concrete, plausible consequence (repeat calls from hang-ups) rather than stretching into a speculative annual cost figure the way the 'overstated' path in the case-sim did.

prompt: "Presenting a baseline number with more decimal places (e.g. 18.37% instead of 18%) makes it more defensible to a skeptical reader."

config.statement: Additional decimal places increase a baseline figure's defensibility.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that false precision — reporting more decimal places than the underlying sample size or method actually supports — tends to undermine credibility with a sharp reader rather than improve it.

hints: What does a figure like 18.37%, drawn from a small, informal sample, imply about the underlying data's precision — and is that implication accurate?
explanation: False. Extra decimal places imply a level of measurement precision the underlying data usually doesn't have — a rate computed from a few weeks of informally logged submissions supports a round number like 18%, not 18.37%, and a skeptical reader who notices the mismatch between implied and actual precision tends to trust the document less, not more.

prompt: Rewrite this baseline line item to be defensible, per this module's standards: "Average handling time: 8 minutes." You don't have real data — invent a plausible method, sample, and period, and state the figure the way a defensible baseline sheet would.
hints: Add a method (how was this measured?), a period or sample size, and, if it's an estimate rather than a logged measurement, a confidence range instead of a single flat number.
explanation: A strong rewrite adds exactly what the flawed Larkspur example was missing: "Average handling time: approximately 8 minutes (measured — logged timestamps on 45 calls sampled across two weeks, March 3-14). Note: sample skews toward weekday daytime calls; weekend volume wasn't separately measured." This states the method (logged timestamps, not recall), the sample size and period (45 calls, two specific weeks), and honestly flags a real limitation of the sample (weekday skew) rather than presenting the figure as a complete, universally-representative measurement.

prompt: A client says a new tool "doubled our throughput." What's the first thing you'd ask?

options.text: What was throughput measured at before the tool was introduced?
How much did the tool cost?
How happy is the team with the tool?

hints: 'Doubled' is a comparison — what's the other half of that comparison?
explanation: Any 'X changed by N' claim needs a before-measurement to be checkable — without it, 'doubled' can't be verified regardless of how the tool is otherwise performing or how much it cost.

prompt: Define 'rework' precisely for a process you're familiar with (pick any real or plausible one), the way this module defines it for Larkspur's referrals.
hints: Rework is about the average number of touches or attempts needed before resolution, not a general sense of redoing work.
explanation: A strong definition names a specific process and a checkable count, e.g.: "For a customer refund request: the average number of times a request is touched (initial review, any clarifying follow-up, final processing) before it's fully resolved, computed from a logged sample over a stated period." The key elements are a precise unit (touches per request) and a real, checkable source, not a vague sense of 'how much redoing happens.'

prompt: "A confident, unmeasured estimate from an experienced staff member is generally close enough to use directly as a baseline number."

config.statement: Confident unmeasured recall from an experienced staff member is close enough to serve directly as a baseline figure.
config.rubric: Accept answers citing the 30-50% typical gap between confident recall and measured figures, and the need to label estimates honestly rather than treat them as equivalent to measured data.

hints: Recall the predict-number exercise's typical gap between confident recall and measured reality.
explanation: False. Confident recall, even from an experienced person, is commonly 30-50% off from a measured figure — it can serve as a useful starting estimate, explicitly labeled as such, but shouldn't be presented or treated as equivalent to an actual measurement.

prompt: Sort each estimation approach into defensible or not defensible, given a process with no existing logged data.

items.text: A two-week forward-looking hand tally of a specific metric
Borrowing a different site's measured rate and presenting it as this site's baseline
A structured recall estimate presented as a range with a stated confidence level
A single confident number from one person's memory, presented with no caveat

hints: The dividing line is whether the technique measures the actual thing in question and is honest about its own certainty.
explanation: A forward-looking tally and an honestly-ranged recall estimate are both defensible because they measure (or honestly estimate) the actual process in question. Borrowing another site's number substitutes a different context's real data for this context's unknown. An uncaveated confident guess misrepresents its own certainty, which is exactly what this module's defensibility lesson warns against.

prompt: Match each finding to who actually absorbs its cost, based on the pattern from this module.

pairs.left: A support ticket takes an extra 3 minutes because the agent looks up account info in a separate system
pairs.right: The agent's time, and the customer's patience while on hold

pairs.left: A rejected insurance submission gets silently resubmitted the same day
pairs.right: The billing coordinator's redo time, and the patient's delayed appointment

pairs.left: A picking error is caught and corrected before a shipment leaves the warehouse
pairs.right: Whoever catches and fixes it, plus any delay to that shipment's schedule

right: Nobody — the process ultimately completed correctly

hints: In each case, ask who spent extra time or experienced extra delay, even though nothing shows up as a customer complaint or a line-item cost.
explanation: Each of these costs is real and absorbed by a specific person or party — agent time and customer patience, coordinator time and patient delay, whoever catches the error plus a shipment's schedule — even though none of them appear as a formal cost anywhere. 'Nobody' is the tempting wrong answer, because the process did technically complete correctly in the end, but 'completed correctly eventually' and 'cost nothing' are not the same claim.

prompt: Put these steps in the order that produces a defensible baseline for a process with no existing clean data.

items: Check whether any real record already exists (even informal) that could be retrospectively sampled
If no usable record exists, set up a short, defined-period forward tally instead of guessing
If neither is possible in the available time, get a structured recall estimate with an explicit range and confidence level
State the method, period or sample size, and confidence level next to every resulting number

hints: Preference order matters: real records first, then forward tally, then honestly-labeled recall as a last resort.
Documentation of method and confidence comes last, applied to whichever technique was actually used.
explanation: Checking for an existing real record first (even an informal one) is the strongest available option if it exists. A forward tally is the next best when no record exists but time allows measuring going forward. A structured, ranged recall estimate is the fallback when neither is possible. Whichever technique was used, stating the method, period, and confidence alongside the resulting number is what makes it defensible, regardless of which of the three techniques produced it.

prompt: A gym's front desk says membership cancellations "usually happen because people just stop coming and eventually cancel." There's no logged reason for any cancellation in the last year. Propose one specific way to start building a defensible baseline on actual cancellation reasons going forward, and name which of this module's estimation techniques it is.
hints: With nothing logged historically and reasons only knowable at the moment of cancellation, which technique fits best going forward?
explanation: A strong answer proposes a time-boxed forward tally: starting now, whoever processes a cancellation logs a brief, standardized reason category (e.g. moved away, cost, stopped using it, switched gyms, other) for every cancellation over a defined period, such as the next two months. This is the forward-looking manual tally technique — the honest answer given the total absence of historical data is that reconstructing the past reliably isn't realistic here, but a modest, low-effort forward measurement will produce real, checkable data going forward.

prompt: A hospital's nursing staff unanimously complain about a clunky medication-dispensing cart interface. Baseline data shows the cart interaction takes about 90 seconds per use; a separate step — waiting for pharmacy to verify a new prescription — averages 45 minutes with no active nursing involvement during the wait. What should you conclude?

options.text: The cart interface is the real problem, since staff complain about it directly
